us015_ac1.design: AutoResponsePolicy { PongInboundPing (default, shipped-Java listener default), Disabled }. The reply is injected when the Ping semantic event is DELIVERED, through the ordinary LocalCommand::SendPong command seam (no duplicated protocol state, no second framing path); its state gate at injection time is Java's own send(Collection) isOpen throw, so a connection that has left Open gets no reply and no failure. Backpressured injections are parked and retried with priority (eof-backpressure-livelock lesson); a fatal injected failure surfaces as DriverOutput::Failure.

Corpus invisibility is proven at the observable level: 74/74 lines byte-identical with runtime excluded, plus corporactl 74/74 exit 0. No stronger claim is possible for ANY change that recompiles ws-core, and none is made.

The US-017 bounded schedule exploration now constructs its drivers under the EXPLICIT AutoResponsePolicy::Disabled configuration (documented in the test): its invariants and byte-pinned retained corpus (fuzz-seeds/us017/minimized/, fuzz-seeds/us017/regressions/) are driver-seam concurrency properties orthogonal to the automatic reply, and they remain valid and green unchanged. The default PongInboundPing behavior is pinned by the dedicated deterministic auto_response.rs suite and the live cross-peer loopback test; the exploration was NOT re-run under the default policy, so no concurrency-exploration claim is made for the auto-pong path.

Driver-seam ordering deltas vs synchronous Java, documented in code and tests: (1) in a single chunk [ping, close], Java pongs before the close echo; the port's core has already queued the close echo when the Ping event drains, so the reply is dropped at the Java isOpen gate — no pong, no failure, close lifecycle untouched. (2) an EOF that latches before the Ping event drains wins the first quiescent turn (pinned US-017 contract) and the reply is dropped — within Java's own envelope, since closeConnection closes the channel without flushing the outQueue. Neither delta is corpus-observable (the corpus never drives the driver).

Pre-open data/control sends refuse with STATE_VIOLATION and POISON the core (the port's uniform partial-execution discipline, same as every fatal code); Java's WebsocketNotConnectedException leaves the connection usable by the caller. This is a JAVA_FAITHFUL_PLUS_SAFE strengthening on a corpus-invisible arm (strictly refuses more), consistent with how the incumbent Unimplemented refusal already poisoned.

The pre-open send_close arm cannot express Java's FLASHPOLICY (-3) branch because the corpus command vocabulary types the requested code as u16; only the 1002 branch and the NEVER_CONNECTED default are reachable, and both are implemented.

Injected auto-pongs consume the core's action/frame budgets (they travel the ordinary command seam); a driver-embedded connection's counters therefore differ from a bare core fed identical inputs. Corpus scoring drives the bare core through ws-oracle-harness, so this is corpus-invisible.

The injection-backpressure retry path (pending_auto_pongs) is defensive: in every schedule we could construct, the byte-path admission bound leaves enough event-queue slack for immediate injection, so no test reaches the parked-retry path; it exists so a refused reply can never be silently lost (the eof-backpressure-livelock lesson).

The handshake exam (49/49) was not re-run: no handshake source changed; the public-tier requests hash equality and 74/74 evaluate are the demanded invariance gates. The full US-018 cross-peer exam was not re-run per instruction; the new loopback test is the cheap cross-peer-style assertion.
